units.title: Court, positions and roles
units.description: Where you stand and what each player does.

cards.title: A court of two halves
cards.body: A volleyball court is 18 m long and 9 m wide. The net splits it into two 9 m by 9 m halves, one for each team. The attack line runs across each half, 3 m from the net.

cards.title: Six zones
cards.body: Each half is split into six zones, numbered 1 to 6. With the net at the top, the front row is 4, 3, 2 from left to right and the back row is 5, 6, 1. Zone 1 is the right back, where the server starts.

questions.prompt: How big is a full volleyball court?
questions.explanation: The court is 18 m long and 9 m wide, so each team gets a 9 m square.

questions.prompt: The attack line is 3 m from the net.
questions.explanation: The attack line is 3 m from the centre line under the net.

questions.prompt: Tap zone 1.
questions.explanation: Zone 1 is the right back, where the server starts.

questions.prompt: Tap zone 4.
questions.explanation: Zone 4 is the left front, next to the net on the left.

questions.prompt: Which zones make up the front row?
questions.explanation: The front row is 4, 3 and 2 from left to right.

questions.prompt: Tap the middle back zone.
questions.explanation: Zone 6 is the middle of the back row.

cards.title: Five roles
cards.body: The setter takes the second contact and sets up the attack. Outside hitters attack from the left and pass the serve. Middle blockers block at the centre of the net. The opposite attacks from the right.

cards.title: The libero
cards.body: The libero is a back-row defensive specialist. They wear a different coloured jersey so officials can spot them, and they usually replace a middle blocker in the back row.

questions.prompt: Match each role to its main job.

pairs.right: Takes the second contact and sets
Attacks from the left and passes serve
Blocks at the centre of the net

questions.explanation: Each role has one main job, which is why teams need all of them.

questions.prompt: Which player wears a different coloured jersey?
questions.explanation: The libero wears a contrasting jersey so officials can track them.

questions.prompt: The setter usually takes the team's second contact.
questions.explanation: The setter takes the second ball and sets it up for a hitter.

questions.prompt: Where does an outside hitter usually attack from?
questions.explanation: Outside hitters attack from the left, zone 4.

questions.prompt: A middle blocker's main job is to block at the centre of the net.
questions.explanation: Middle blockers stand in the middle so they can reach blocks on both sides.

cards.title: The lineup
cards.body: Before each set, the coach records the starting order of the six players. That order stays the same for the whole set, even as players move around.

cards.title: Rotating
cards.body: When your team wins the serve back from the other team, everyone moves one zone clockwise. The player who moves from zone 2 to zone 1 serves next.

questions.prompt: A team rotates every time it wins a rally.
questions.explanation: A team only rotates when it wins the serve back from the other team.

questions.prompt: When your team rotates, the player in zone 2 moves to which zone?
questions.explanation: Rotation is clockwise, so zone 2 moves back to zone 1.

questions.prompt: A player in zone 4 rotates once. Tap the zone they move to.
questions.explanation: Clockwise, zone 4 moves to zone 3.

questions.prompt: Who serves after your team rotates?
options: The player who moved into zone 1
questions.answer: The player who moved into zone 1
questions.explanation: The player who rotates into zone 1 serves.

questions.prompt: The starting order can change in the middle of a set.
questions.explanation: The rotation order is set at the start of each set and stays the same.

questions.prompt: The lineup in zones 1 to 6 is S, OH1, MB1, OPP, OH2, MB2. Place each player.
questions.explanation: The lineup fills zones 1 to 6 in order, starting with the setter in zone 1.

questions.prompt: The same lineup rotates once. Place each player.
questions.explanation: Everyone moves one zone clockwise, so OH1 moves from zone 2 to zone 1 to serve.

units.title: Rules and terminology
units.description: How points are won and the words players use.

cards.title: Three contacts
cards.body: A team can touch the ball up to three times before sending it over. A block does not count as one of those three, and the same player cannot touch the ball twice in a row.

cards.title: Rally scoring
cards.body: Every rally scores a point, no matter which team served. A set is won at 25 points with a two-point lead. A deciding fifth set goes to 15.

questions.prompt: How many times can a team touch the ball before sending it over?
questions.explanation: A team gets up to three contacts, not counting the block.

questions.prompt: A block counts as one of the team's three contacts.
questions.explanation: A block does not count, so a team still has three contacts after it.

questions.prompt: A team scores a point on every rally, whether or not it served.
questions.explanation: This is called rally scoring.

questions.prompt: How is a regular set won?
questions.explanation: A set goes to 25, and you must lead by two.

questions.prompt: A deciding fifth set is played to how many points?
questions.explanation: The fifth set is shorter: 15 points with a two-point lead.

cards.title: The net
cards.body: Touching the net between the antennae while playing the ball is a fault. The ball must cross the net between the antennae.

cards.title: Lines and the centre line
cards.body: A ball that lands on a boundary line is in. A foot may cross the centre line under the net as long as part of it stays on or above the line.

questions.prompt: Touching the net between the antennae while playing the ball is a fault.
questions.explanation: Contact with the net while playing the ball is a fault.

questions.prompt: A foot may touch the other team's court if part of it stays on or above the centre line.
questions.explanation: Part of the foot must stay on or directly above the centre line.

questions.prompt: Where must the ball cross the net?
questions.explanation: The crossing space is between the antennae.

questions.prompt: A ball lands on the boundary line. Is it in or out?
questions.explanation: The lines are part of the court, so the ball is in.

questions.prompt: A player may hit the ball twice in a row.
questions.explanation: One player cannot make two contacts in a row, except at the block or in one action on the first team contact.

cards.title: Words for good plays
cards.body: An ace is a serve that scores directly. A kill is an attack that ends the rally. A dig is a pass of a hard attack.

cards.title: Words for the flow of play
cards.body: A side-out is winning the rally while receiving. A free ball is an easy ball sent over without an attack. An overpass is a pass that goes straight over the net.

questions.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.right: An attack that ends the rally
A pass of a hard-driven attack

questions.explanation: These words come up in every practice and game.

questions.prompt: What is a free ball?
options: An easy ball sent over without an attack
A ball that hits the antenna
questions.answer: An easy ball sent over without an attack
questions.explanation: A free ball gives the other team an easy chance to set up an attack.

questions.prompt: What is an overpass?
options: A pass that goes straight over the net
A set to the back row
questions.answer: A pass that goes straight over the net
questions.explanation: An overpass gives the other team an easy attack.

questions.prompt: A side-out happens when the receiving team wins the rally.
questions.explanation: Winning the rally while receiving earns a point and the serve.

questions.prompt: A back-row player may attack from behind the attack line.
questions.explanation: Back-row players can attack as long as they take off from behind the attack line.

units.title: Rotations, overlap and serving
units.description: The order players stand in and how it changes.

cards.title: Order at the serve
cards.body: When the ball is served, the receiving team must stand in its rotation order. Under the current FIVB rules, the serving team does not have to.

cards.title: What overlap means
cards.body: Each front-row player must be closer to the net than the back-row player behind them (4 ahead of 5, 3 ahead of 6, 2 ahead of 1). In each row, players must also keep their left-to-right order. Feet on the floor decide position.

questions.prompt: Under FIVB rules, only the receiving team must be in rotation order when the ball is served.
questions.explanation: The current FIVB rules apply rotation order at the serve to the receiving team only.
questions.leagueNote: Many recreational leagues still require both teams to be in order.

questions.prompt: At the serve, the player in zone 3 must be closer to the net than the player in which zone?
questions.explanation: Each front-row player must be ahead of the back-row player behind them, and 6 is behind 3.

questions.prompt: At the serve, where must the player in zone 6 stand, left to right?
options: Between the players in zones 5 and 1
questions.answer: Between the players in zones 5 and 1
questions.explanation: In the back row, the left-to-right order is 5, 6, 1.

questions.prompt: Positions are judged by where players' feet touch the floor.
questions.explanation: Overlap is judged by the position of the feet on the floor.

questions.prompt: After the ball is served, players may move anywhere on their own side.
questions.explanation: Rotation order only applies at the moment of the serve.

cards.title: The serve
cards.body: The server stands behind the end line and has 8 seconds after the whistle to serve. They may not touch the court or the end line when they hit the ball.

cards.title: Serving order
cards.body: The serve follows the rotation order. A serve that touches the net and still goes over is in play.

questions.prompt: How long does the server have after the whistle?
questions.explanation: The server must hit the ball within 8 seconds of the whistle.

questions.prompt: The server may step on the end line while hitting the serve.
questions.explanation: At the moment of the serve, the server may not touch the court or the end line.

questions.prompt: Tap the zone of the player who serves.
questions.explanation: The player in zone 1 serves.

questions.prompt: A serve that touches the net and still goes over is in play.
questions.explanation: A net serve that crosses into the other court is a legal serve.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a serving fault?
options: Serving from the left of the service zone
questions.explanation: The serve must follow the rotation order. The other options are allowed.

cards.title: A back-row specialist
cards.body: The libero may only play in the back row, zones 5, 6 and 1. They may not block or attempt to block.

cards.title: Replacements
cards.body: The libero usually comes in for a middle blocker who has rotated to the back row. These swaps are called replacements, and they do not count as substitutions.

questions.prompt: Which zones can the libero play in?
questions.explanation: The libero is limited to the back row.

questions.prompt: The libero may block or attempt to block.
questions.explanation: The libero may not block or attempt to block.

questions.prompt: Which player does the libero usually replace?
options: A middle blocker in the back row
An outside hitter in the front row
questions.answer: A middle blocker in the back row
questions.explanation: Middles are tall blockers, so the libero takes over their back-row defence.

questions.prompt: Libero replacements count as substitutions.
questions.explanation: Replacements involving the libero are not counted as substitutions.

questions.prompt: The libero replaces a middle in the middle back. Tap that zone.
questions.explanation: The middle back is zone 6.

questions.prompt: The lineup in zones 1 to 6 is S, OH1, MB1, OPP, OH2, MB2. The libero replaces the back-row middle. Place each player.
questions.explanation: MB2 starts in zone 6, a back-row zone, so the libero takes that spot.

questions.prompt: In rotation 1 the back row is S in zone 1, OH2 in zone 5 and a middle blocker in zone 6. The libero comes in for the middle. Place the back row.
questions.explanation: The libero replaces the back-row middle in zone 6, and nobody else moves.

units.title: The 5-1 system
units.description: The most common team system, one setter and five hitters.

cards.title: One setter, five hitters
cards.body: A 5-1 uses one setter in all six rotations and five hitters: two outside hitters, two middle blockers and one opposite.

cards.title: Across from each other
cards.body: In the lineup, the setter is across from the opposite, the two outside hitters are across from each other, and the two middle blockers are across from each other. Across means three zones apart.

questions.prompt: In a 5-1, how many setters are on the court?
questions.explanation: The "1" in 5-1 is the single setter.

questions.prompt: Why is it called a 5-1?
options: Five front-row players and one back-row player
questions.explanation: A 5-1 has five hitters and one setter.

questions.prompt: Match each player to the player across the rotation from them.
questions.explanation: Players who are across from each other are always three zones apart.

questions.prompt: In a 5-1, the two outside hitters are across from each other in the lineup.
questions.explanation: This keeps one outside hitter in the front row at all times.

questions.prompt: In a 5-1, the setter starts in zone 1. Place the setter and the opposite.
questions.explanation: The opposite is always three zones away from the setter, so zone 4.

questions.prompt: The setter is in zone 1, OH1 in zone 2 and MB1 in zone 3. Place each partner three zones away from them.
questions.explanation: Partners are three zones apart: the opposite in 4, the other outside hitter in 5 and the other middle in 6.

lessons.title: Setter front row, setter back row

cards.title: Setter in the back row
cards.body: When the setter is in the back row, all three front-row players can attack. The setter moves forward to set from the right front.

cards.title: Setter in the front row
cards.body: When the setter is in the front row, only two front-row players are hitters. The setter can still attack, but usually sets.

questions.prompt: When the setter is in the back row, how many front-row hitters are there?
questions.explanation: All three front-row players can attack.

questions.prompt: When the setter is in the front row, how many front-row hitters are there?
questions.explanation: The setter takes one front-row spot, leaving two hitters.

questions.prompt: A back-row setter may attack a ball that is fully above the net from in front of the attack line.
questions.explanation: A back-row player may not complete an attack above the net from the front zone.

questions.prompt: The setter is in zone 1. Tap the opposite's zone.
questions.explanation: The opposite is three zones away from the setter, so zone 4.

questions.prompt: The setter is in zone 6. Tap the opposite's zone.
questions.explanation: Three zones away from zone 6 is zone 3.

questions.prompt: The setter is in zone 4, in the front row. Place the setter and the opposite.
questions.explanation: Three zones away from zone 4 is zone 1, so the opposite is in the back row.

cards.title: Naming rotations
cards.body: Many teams name each rotation by the setter's zone. In rotation 1 the setter is in zone 1.

cards.title: The cycle
cards.body: Each rotation moves the setter one zone clockwise: from zone 1 to 6, then 5, 4, 3 and 2, and back to 1.

questions.prompt: Many teams name a rotation by what?
questions.explanation: Rotation 1 means the setter is in zone 1.

questions.prompt: From rotation 1, the team rotates once. Which zone is the setter in now?
questions.explanation: Clockwise, zone 1 moves to zone 6.

questions.prompt: In a 5-1, the setter never plays in the front row.
questions.explanation: The setter rotates through all six zones, front and back.

questions.prompt: An outside hitter is in zone 2. The team rotates once. Tap their new zone.
questions.explanation: Clockwise, zone 2 moves to zone 1.

questions.prompt: Starting from rotation 1, which rotation first puts the setter in the front row?
questions.explanation: The setter moves 1, 6, 5, then 4, the first front-row zone.

questions.prompt: The setter is in zone 5. The order around the lineup is S, OH1, MB1, OPP, OH2, MB2. Place each player.
questions.explanation: Each player follows the one before in zone order: 5, 6, 1, 2, 3, 4.

glossary.definition: A system with two setters, each setting from the front row, and four hitters. Common with newer teams.
glossary.example: A 4-2 keeps things simple, but only two players attack in each rotation.

glossary.definition: A system with one setter in all six rotations and five hitters: two outside hitters, two middle blockers and one opposite.
glossary.example: In a 5-1, the setter is across the lineup from the opposite.

glossary.definition: A system with two setters, each setting only from the back row, so there are always three front-row hitters.
glossary.example: In a 6-2, the setter who rotates to the front row becomes a hitter.

glossary.definition: A serve that scores directly, with no successful pass by the receiving team.
glossary.example: The server earned an ace when the ball dropped between two passers.

glossary.definition: A flexible rod fixed to each side of the net. It marks the side edge of the space the ball must cross.
glossary.example: A ball that touches the antenna is out.

glossary.definition: A player using a teammate or any object to reach the ball. It is a fault.
glossary.example: Pushing off a teammate to jump higher for a dig is an assisted hit.

glossary.definition: Any action that sends the ball toward the opponent, except a serve or a block.
glossary.example: A spike, a tip and a roll shot are all attack hits.

glossary.definition: The line 3 m from the centre line on each side. It separates the front zone from the back zone.
glossary.example: A back-row player must take off from behind the attack line to attack above the net.

glossary.definition: The three players in zones 5, 6 and 1 at the serve. They may not block, and must attack from behind the attack line.
glossary.example: A back-row player who jumps from behind the attack line may attack above the net.

glossary.definition: An attack by a back-row player. It is legal only if the player takes off from behind the attack line when the ball is fully above the net.
glossary.example: The opposite hit a back-row attack from behind the attack line.

glossary.definition: A back-row player or the libero completing or attempting a block. It is a fault.
glossary.example: The setter in zone 1 may not join the block.

glossary.definition: The area behind the attack line, up to the end line.
glossary.example: The libero usually plays in the back zone.

glossary.definition: Where a player goes after the serve to play their role.
glossary.example: A setter's base position is the right front, between zones 2 and 3.

glossary.definition: Players close to the net reaching above it to stop the opponent's attack. Only front-row players may complete a block, and a block touch does not count as a team contact.
glossary.example: After a block touch, the team still has three contacts.

glossary.definition: Everyday name for the forearm pass.
glossary.example: Bump it high to the setter.

glossary.definition: The player who speaks for the team with the referees.
glossary.example: Only the game captain may ask the referee to explain a call during play.

glossary.definition: When the ball is caught or thrown instead of being hit. It is a fault.
glossary.example: A tip that is held in the hand before being pushed over is a catch.

glossary.definition: The line under the net that splits the court into two halves.
glossary.example: A foot may cross the centre line only if part of it stays on or above the line.

glossary.definition: Crossing into the opponent's court in a way that is not allowed, such as with the whole foot or by interfering with their play.
glossary.example: Landing with your whole foot past the centre line is a fault.

glossary.definition: Any touch of the ball by a player.
glossary.example: A team may make up to three contacts before sending the ball over.

glossary.definition: The 18 m by 9 m playing area. The net splits it into two 9 m by 9 m halves, one per team.
glossary.example: Each team defends its own half of the court.

glossary.definition: Teammates moving close to their own attacker to dig a ball that is blocked back.
glossary.example: Good cover turned the blocked spike into a second attack.

glossary.definition: The part of the vertical plane of the net, between the antennae and below the ceiling, that the ball must pass through to go to the other side.
glossary.example: A ball that goes outside the antenna has not crossed in the crossing space.

glossary.definition: The fifth set, played to 15 points with a two-point lead.
glossary.example: In the deciding set, teams switch sides at 8 points.

glossary.definition: A substitute who comes in to pass and defend. Unlike the libero, they follow normal substitution rules.
glossary.example: A coach may sub in a defensive specialist for a front-row hitter who rotates to the back.

glossary.definition: A pass of a hard-driven attack, usually close to the floor.
glossary.example: The libero dug the spike and kept the rally alive.

glossary.definition: One player touching the ball twice in a row, or the ball touching several parts of their body one after another. It is a fault, except at the block and on the first team contact in one action.
glossary.example: A setter who touches the ball twice in a row has made a double contact.

glossary.definition: When both teams commit a fault at the same time. The rally is replayed.
glossary.example: Both players touching the net at once is a double fault.

glossary.definition: An attack hit from a standing position or a small jump, used when a full spike is not possible.
glossary.example: After a poor pass, the hitter sent a down ball deep to zone 1.

glossary.definition: The line at the back of each half of the court.
glossary.example: The server must not touch the end line when hitting the serve.

glossary.definition: A rules violation. It ends the rally and gives the other team the point.
glossary.example: Four touches is a fault even if the last one goes over.

glossary.definition: The official on the stand at one end of the net who starts each rally and has the final say.
glossary.example: The first referee whistles for the serve.

glossary.definition: A serve hit with little or no spin, so it moves unpredictably in the air.
glossary.example: A good float serve can be hard to pass because it wobbles.

glossary.definition: Touching the court or the end line at the moment of the serve hit, or the take-off for a jump serve.
glossary.example: He stepped on the end line as he served, so it was a foot fault.

glossary.definition: Playing the ball off the forearms held together. Often called a bump.
glossary.example: Most serves are received with a forearm pass.

glossary.definition: A team touching the ball four times before sending it over. It is a fault.
glossary.example: Pass, set, hit, then one more touch before the ball crosses is four hits.

glossary.definition: A call that the opponent is about to send an easy ball over.
glossary.example: When the other team only bumps it over, call "Free!" and drop off the net.

glossary.definition: An easy ball sent over without an attack, often with a forearm pass.
glossary.example: On a free ball, blockers drop back from the net to get ready to attack.

glossary.definition: The space around the court where players may still play the ball.
glossary.example: A player can chase a ball into the free zone and send it back.

glossary.definition: The three players in zones 4, 3 and 2 at the serve. They may block and attack from anywhere.
glossary.example: When the setter is in the front row, there are only two front-row hitters.

glossary.definition: The area between the centre line and the attack line.
glossary.example: Back-row players may not complete an attack above the net from the front zone.

glossary.definition: A ball that lands on or inside the boundary lines. The lines are part of the court.
glossary.example: The ball clipped the end line, so it was in.

glossary.definition: When players from both teams contact the ball above the net at the same time. Play continues.
glossary.example: After the joust, the ball fell on the blue team's side, so they kept playing it.

glossary.definition: A serve hit while jumping, usually with topspin and power.
glossary.example: The server may land inside the court after hitting a jump serve.

glossary.definition: An attack that ends the rally in the attacking team's favour.
glossary.example: The middle blocker scored a kill on a quick set.

glossary.definition: A back-row defensive specialist in a different coloured jersey. The libero may only play in the back row and may not block, attempt to block or serve.
glossary.example: The libero comes in for the middle blocker when the middle rotates to the back row.

glossary.definition: When the libero swaps in or out for a back-row player. Replacements are unlimited and are not counted as substitutions.
glossary.example: The libero replaces the middle blocker after the middle serves or rotates out.

glossary.definition: A ball that is held, caught or thrown instead of hit cleanly. The rules call it a catch.
glossary.example: The ref called a lift on the one-handed save.

glossary.definition: An official who uses a flag to signal whether a ball is in or out.
glossary.example: The line judge flagged the serve out.

glossary.definition: The starting order of the six players, recorded on the line-up sheet before each set. It stays the same for the whole set.
glossary.example: A lineup of S, OH1, MB1, OPP, OH2, MB2 puts the setter in zone 1.

glossary.definition: A contest of up to five sets. The first team to win three sets wins the match.
glossary.example: The match went to five sets.

glossary.definition: A player who blocks at the centre of the net and attacks quick sets.
glossary.example: The libero often replaces the middle blocker in the back row.

glossary.definition: A call that means "I will take this ball," so teammates do not collide.
glossary.example: Call "Mine!" early on every pass you take.

glossary.definition: The barrier across the middle of the court. The ball must go over it, between the antennae.
glossary.example: Touching the net between the antennae while playing the ball is a fault.

glossary.definition: Touching the net between the antennae while playing the ball. Touching it when not playing the ball is not a fault, as long as it does not interfere with play.
glossary.example: Brushing the top of the net while blocking is a net fault.

glossary.definition: 2.43 m for men and 2.24 m for women in senior play.
glossary.example: Youth and recreational leagues often use a lower net.

glossary.definition: A serve that touches the net and still goes over. It is in play.
glossary.example: The net serve trickled over and the receivers had to scramble.

glossary.definition: The player across the lineup from the setter. They attack mainly from the right side.
glossary.example: In a 5-1, the opposite is always three zones away from the setter.

glossary.definition: A ball that lands outside the lines, touches an antenna, or hits something outside the court such as the ceiling or a wall.
glossary.example: The serve hit the ceiling, so it was out.

glossary.definition: A player who attacks mainly from the left side (zone 4) and helps pass the serve.
glossary.example: Teams usually have two outside hitters across from each other in the lineup.

glossary.definition: Playing the ball above the head with the fingers of both hands.
glossary.example: Setters use an overhead pass to set the ball.

glossary.definition: Being out of place relative to a neighbour at the serve, such as a back-row player standing ahead of the front-row player in front of them.
glossary.example: The player in zone 6 must be behind the player in zone 3 when the ball is served.

glossary.definition: A pass that goes straight over the net, giving the opponent an easy attack.
glossary.example: A hard serve forced an overpass, and the front row hit it straight down.

glossary.definition: Usually the first contact, sending the ball to the setter.
glossary.example: A good pass lets the setter choose any hitter.

glossary.definition: A back-row setter running forward to the net right after the serve to set.
glossary.example: When the setter is in zone 1, they penetrate to the right front to set.

glossary.definition: A back-row attack from the middle of the court, around zone 6.
glossary.example: The outside hitter ran a pipe while the front row distracted the block.

glossary.definition: The flat surface made by joining your hands and locking your forearms to pass.
glossary.example: Keep your platform angled at the setter.

glossary.definition: A player is not in their correct position when the ball is served. The other team gets the point and the serve.
glossary.example: Standing ahead of your front-row teammate at the serve is a positional fault.

glossary.definition: A fast, low set to the middle blocker, who is already in the air.
glossary.example: The middle hit a quick set before the block could form.

glossary.definition: The play from the serve until the ball is out of play.
glossary.example: The rally ended when the ball landed in.

glossary.definition: Every rally scores a point, whichever team served.
glossary.example: With rally scoring, a mistake on your own serve still gives the other team a point.

glossary.definition: A blocker may reach beyond the net, but must not touch the ball on the opponent's side before or during the opponent's attack hit.
glossary.example: Blocking a ball the hitter has already attacked is legal even if your hands are over the net.

glossary.definition: A rally played again, for example when both teams commit faults at the same time.
glossary.example: After a double fault, the referee called for a replay.

glossary.definition: An attack hit with a slow, looping arm swing so the ball drops behind the block.
glossary.example: The hitter used a roll shot over the block into zone 6.

glossary.definition: Moving one zone clockwise when your team wins the serve back. The player who moves from zone 2 to zone 1 serves next.
glossary.example: After a side-out, everyone rotates before the next serve.

glossary.definition: Serving out of the rotation order. The other team gets the point and the serve.
glossary.example: If the wrong player serves, it is a rotational fault.

glossary.definition: The order set by the lineup, which players must keep at the moment of the serve (receiving team).
glossary.example: Under FIVB rules, only the receiving team must be in rotational order at the serve.

glossary.definition: When players of the serving team block the receivers' view of the server or the ball's path. It is a fault.
glossary.example: Teammates bunching up in front of the server to hide the serve can be called for a screen.

glossary.definition: The official on the floor across from the first referee who watches the net, the centre line and substitutions.
glossary.example: The second referee called the net fault.

glossary.definition: The hit that puts the ball into play, made by the right-back player from the service zone.
glossary.example: The server has 8 seconds after the whistle to serve.

glossary.definition: The player who serves: whoever is in zone 1 when the rally starts.
glossary.example: After a side-out, the player who rotates into zone 1 becomes the server.

glossary.definition: The formation the receiving team uses to pass the serve.
glossary.example: In serve receive, the setter is often stacked near the right side.

glossary.definition: A serve that lands out, fails to cross the net, or touches an antenna. The other team scores.
glossary.example: Hitting the serve into the net is a service error.

glossary.definition: The order in which players serve, which follows the lineup.
glossary.example: Serving out of order is a rotational fault.

glossary.definition: The server must hit the ball within 8 seconds of the first referee's whistle.
glossary.example: Taking too long to serve gives the point to the other team.

glossary.definition: The 9 m wide area behind the end line where the server stands.
glossary.example: The server can serve from anywhere inside the service zone.

glossary.definition: The contact that places the ball for a teammate to attack, usually the second contact.
glossary.example: A high set to the outside gives the hitter time to approach.

glossary.definition: A game within a match, won by the first team to 25 points with a two-point lead.
glossary.example: The team won the first set 25 to 22.

glossary.definition: The player who usually takes the second contact and sets the ball up for a hitter.
glossary.example: In a 5-1, one setter sets in all six rotations.

glossary.definition: The setter attacks the second ball instead of setting it. A back-row setter may not complete this attack from in front of the attack line with the ball fully above the net.
glossary.example: A front-row setter can dump the ball over when the block is not ready.

glossary.definition: A badly mis-hit pass that goes far from the target.
glossary.example: The serve hit his wrist and he shanked it into the stands.

glossary.definition: The two lines along the long sides of the court.
glossary.example: A ball that lands on the sideline is in.

glossary.definition: Winning the rally while receiving. The receiving team scores and earns the serve.
glossary.example: A side-out means your team rotates before serving.

glossary.definition: A powerful attack hit from above the net.
glossary.example: The outside hitter spiked the ball cross-court for a kill.

glossary.definition: Arranging players at the serve so they can switch quickly while still staying in legal order.
glossary.example: Teams often stack the setter close to the right side in serve receive.

glossary.definition: A block that sends the ball straight down onto the attacker's side for a point.
glossary.example: The middle stuff-blocked the quick set.

glossary.definition: Replacing one player with another during a set. Libero replacements do not count as substitutions.
glossary.example: A team gets a limited number of regular substitutions each set.

glossary.definition: Moving to your playing spot right after the serve. It is legal because players may move anywhere once the ball is served.
glossary.example: The setter switches to the right front after the serve to set.

glossary.definition: A team may touch the ball up to three times before it must cross the net. A block does not count as one of the three.
glossary.example: Pass, set, hit is the classic three-contact play.

glossary.definition: A 30-second break requested by a team. Each team may take up to two per set.
glossary.example: The coach called a timeout to reset after three straight points.

glossary.definition: A soft attack pushed over or around the block with the fingertips. It must not be caught or thrown.
glossary.example: A tip into the middle of the court can catch the defence off guard.

glossary.definition: An attack hit off the block so it lands out of bounds. The point goes to the attacking team.
glossary.example: The hitter tooled the block and the ball landed out past the sideline.

glossary.definition: A serve with forward spin that dives down quickly.
glossary.example: The topspin serve dropped right inside the end line.

glossary.definition: Switching from defence to attack, or back, during a rally.
glossary.example: After the dig, the team transitioned and the setter ran in to set.

glossary.definition: A serve hit from below the waist with an open hand or fist. It is legal in all levels of play.
glossary.example: Many new players start with an underhand serve.

glossary.definition: The six areas of each half, numbered 1 to 6. With the net at the top, the front row is 4, 3, 2 and the back row is 5, 6, 1.
glossary.example: Zone 1 is the right back, where the server starts.
